title: How to Organize Reference Images for Design Work
description: Organize reference images for your next design: a practical workflow, a PureRef, Eagle, Milanote and FloatBoard comparison, and tips for keeping notes beside images.
alt: FloatBoard in dark mode displaying four landscape image references in a two-column grid
caption: A four-image board keeps a small set of references visible together. This screenshot shows the FloatBoard image layout; the workflow below is an illustrative example.
intro: To organize reference images for design work, keep your original files in a searchable project folder, then choose a small working set for the decision in front of you. This guide is for designers and illustrators who need to compare composition, light or visual direction while drawing. It walks through a four-image example in FloatBoard and explains when PureRef, Eagle or Milanote may fit better.

sections.title: Start with a design question, not a pile of pictures
sections.html:
Before adding images, write one sentence describing the decision you need to make. For example: ‘Choose a warm evening palette with a quiet, open composition.’ This gives every image a job. One might show the light, another the amount of empty space, and another the contrast between foreground and background.

The screenshot above contains four different landscapes. For this example, the coastal sunset can be a reference for warm light, the palm scene for reflections, the mountain scene for silhouette, and the darker landscape for contrast. Those are observations to compare, not four instructions to reproduce in one design.

If you cannot explain why an image is on your board, leave it in your source folder for now. A small board that answers one question is easier to use than a larger board whose images compete for attention.

sections.title: Keep reference images and notes visible in FloatBoard
sections.html:
1. Keep the originals. Save your source files in a project folder. Treat the board as a working reference, not your only archive.
  2. Choose a few distinct references. Avoid filling the board with almost identical images. Pick the examples that reveal different aspects of your question.
  3. Add the images to FloatBoard. Use the image workflow available in your installed version. The image panel keeps the references together, as shown in the screenshot.
  4. Place the window beside your canvas. Use the pin / always-on-top control so the board remains visible when you return to the design app. Leave enough space for the actual work.
  5. Add a short reference note. In the text panel, write the design question and one observation per image. Keep copied client wording labelled separately from your own ideas; a clipboard fragment needs its source and context.
  6. Check readability. If important details are too small, work with fewer references or use a larger view. A tiny thumbnail is suitable for overall composition, but not fine typography or texture.

FloatBoard’s free plan has image limits. Check the current plan details before planning a larger collection; this workflow does not require filling every available slot.

sections.title: Record what each reference teaches you
sections.html:
Images alone do not preserve the reasoning behind a design. Keep a short note in your project document with three fields: source, detail to study, and decision. For example: ‘Coastal sunset — warm highlights against a darker foreground — try a warm accent on a neutral background.’

Save the source URL and any usage or licensing information with the original. Collecting an image for reference does not give you permission to publish it. When it is time to deliver the project, choose assets you own or have permission to use.

After each design pass, write down which reference helped. If two images now serve the same purpose, keep the clearer one on the working board. This makes the next pass a focused comparison instead of another round of browsing.

sections.title: Fix the common problems before adding more images
sections.html:
The board covers your work: move or resize it rather than squeezing your canvas into the remaining space. On a small screen, it can be more useful to compare two images at a time.

You keep collecting but do not decide: return to the opening question. Choose one visual direction, make a small draft, and compare that draft against your references. The board supports a decision; it does not make one.

You need precise color values: return to the original asset and your design app’s color tools. A scaled screenshot or thumbnail should not be treated as an authoritative color measurement.

sections.title: Tools for this workflow: PureRef, Eagle, Milanote or FloatBoard?
sections.html:
Choose a reference image organizer by the job you need it to do. Keeping pictures above your canvas, finding an old asset and presenting a mood board are different needs. The suggestions below are based on the linked product documentation, checked on 24 September 2026; they are not a hands-on comparison or a speed benchmark. This guide is published by FloatBoard.

Which tool fits your reference-image workflow?
ToolConsider it whenWhat to check
PureRefYour main task is arranging visual references and keeping them above a drawing app. Its reference-viewing features include always-on-top.Choose the appropriate personal or commercial license. Start here if a dedicated reference canvas is your priority.
EagleYou need to retrieve assets across many projects. Its organizing tools include tags, folders and smart folders.Decide how you will label and maintain the library. A catalog and a small on-screen working set can serve complementary roles.
MilanoteYou want to explain visual direction to someone else. Its mood boards support sharing and comments.Check sharing permissions and plan limits before building a large client board.
FloatBoardYou want a small set of images beside desktop notes or copied text, with an always-on-top window while you work.The free plan allows 5 texts and 5 images per day and one window. This image grid is not a substitute for a full asset catalog or shared review tool.

If you arrived looking for a PureRef alternative, identify what you want to change first. For a mixed notes-and-images workspace, try FloatBoard with one task. For asset retrieval, investigate Eagle; for shared feedback, investigate Milanote. These tools are not interchangeable replacements for every PureRef feature.

sections.title: Is PureRef free? Check the license before choosing an alternative
sections.html:
PureRef’s download page currently offers a custom contribution amount for its personal, hobbyist and educational license, and separate paid commercial options. Do not assume that personal-use terms cover paid client work; check the current download options and license agreement for your situation.

If you want to try a different workflow without paying first, FloatBoard has the limited free plan described above. Milanote’s free plan includes 100 notes, images or links and 10 file uploads. Those limits measure different things, so compare them against your actual project rather than treating either as an unlimited reference library.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions about organizing reference images
sections.html:
What is the best way to organize reference images?

Separate storage from active reference. Keep original files and source links in project folders, use descriptive names or tags for retrieval, and bring only the images needed for the current decision onto your working board. For example, tag an image by what you need to find later—lighting, composition or material—not just “inspiration.”

Is there a free alternative to PureRef?

For a small mixed board of notes and images, you can try FloatBoard’s free plan. For a shareable mood board, Milanote has a free tier. Neither choice reproduces every PureRef feature; choose based on whether you need a visible reference, an asset library or collaboration, and check the limits above.

How do I keep reference images visible while drawing?

Use an always-on-top reference window, position it beside your canvas and switch back to the drawing app to check the layout. FloatBoard and PureRef support this approach. If the board hides your tools, reduce the working set or move it to another display.

Can I keep design notes beside my reference images?

Yes. FloatBoard’s text and image panels can share a window. Try one note containing your brief, source links and the next decision beside a few selected images. For longer written work, follow the guide to keeping reference notes visible; for interface work, see code snippets and screenshots while debugging.

sections.title: Try the workflow with your next design task
sections.html:
Download FloatBoard, choose up to four reference images and add one note describing the decision you are making. Pin the board beside your design app, make a draft, then remove any reference that no longer helps. Keep final decisions in your project document so they survive beyond this working set.

If copied instructions are what you lose most often, explore the clipboard manager workflow. If your priority is written reminders above other windows, start with floating desktop notes. Use the board for the material you need in sight now.

title: How to Debug UI Bugs with Code Snippets and Screenshots
description: Keep a screenshot, code snippet and expected result together while debugging UI bugs. Compare FloatBoard with snippet managers for this specific workflow.
alt: FloatBoard with four image thumbnails on the left and a text card containing HTML markup on the right
caption: FloatBoard can show image references and text side by side. The HTML in this screenshot is a reference snippet, not an executable code editor.
intro: If you are debugging a visual bug, a searchable code snippet manager and a visible reference board solve different problems. Keep reusable code in your repository or snippet library; put the screenshot, the few relevant lines and the expected result in view for the bug you are fixing now. Here is a repeatable UI-debugging workflow, followed by an honest comparison with massCode, Pieces and Cacher.

sections.title: Start with one reproducible UI bug
sections.html:
First write down the action that triggers the bug, the viewport or window size and what actually happens. Then record the expected behavior. A screenshot without these details can look convincing but leave a teammate unable to reproduce anything.

Keep the screenshot in your issue or project folder, where it will still be available after this working session. Copy only the smallest relevant markup or CSS fragment onto your temporary board. Label it with the file path and component name so you can return to the authoritative source.

Do not paste access tokens, customer data or private URLs into a board that may appear in a screen share. Redact the screenshot before sharing it.

sections.title: Put a screenshot and code snippet side by side
sections.html:
1. Capture the visual symptom. Make one screenshot at the size where the problem appears. Keep the original in the bug report.
  2. Copy the relevant snippet. Add its file path and a brief note about why you suspect it. A text card is a reference, not a synchronized copy of the source file.
  3. Add both to FloatBoard. Put the screenshot in the image panel and the snippet plus expected result in the text panel. The image above shows this mixed layout.
  4. Pin the board beside the editor. Keep it in view while the editor and browser remain the tools you use to change and test the code.
  5. Change one likely cause and reproduce again. Replace the working note with the new observation; do not stack unexplained copies of the same snippet.

This is useful when you need a snippet manager with images for the immediate task. FloatBoard is not a searchable code library or an IDE: it does not run code, highlight syntax or keep pasted text in sync with Git.

sections.title: Example: debug an overflowing image grid at 390px
sections.html:
Suppose a gallery extends past its container on a narrow screen. The note below keeps the question, evidence and next check together. It is an illustrative checklist, not a diagnosis of FloatBoard or a universal CSS fix.

Bug: image cards overflow the gallery panel
Reproduce: open the gallery at a 390px viewport
Actual: horizontal scrolling appears
Expected: cards stay inside the panel
Source: styles/gallery.css, .gallery-grid
Evidence: screenshot saved in issue #123
Next check: grid columns, item min-width, image sizing

In DevTools, inspect the actual grid and its children. If a child cannot shrink, test whether its minimum size causes the overflow; if the column definition is fixed, test a responsive layout. Keep the before and after screenshots at the same viewport. The fix belongs in the source and its test, not in the reference note.

sections.title: Snippet manager or floating board? Choose by the job
sections.html:
A code snippet manager is a better place for examples you want to search and reuse next month. A floating board is for the few references you must compare while fixing one bug today. This is a feature-and-use-case comparison based on the linked product documentation, checked on 28 September 2026; we did not benchmark the competing apps. FloatBoard publishes this guide.

Where to keep snippets and screenshots
ToolUseful whenImage and code context
massCodeYou need a searchable, reusable local snippet library. Its Code workspace supports folders, tags and search.Its Notes and Drawings can contain visual material. Do not treat it as a text-only app.
PiecesYou need capture and retrieval features beyond a small working board.Pieces documents image pasting and code extraction from screenshots. Check its current product and plan before choosing it.
CacherYou want a searchable code library, editor integrations or team snippets. Its documentation describes search and insertion.Its attachments support pasted images. Do not assume a snippet manager cannot store screenshots.
FloatBoardYou want a small screenshot and text reference visible above your editor while investigating one issue.Separate image and text panels sit in one always-on-top window. There is no code-library search or syntax highlighting. The free plan allows 5 texts and 5 images per day.

Looking for a massCode alternative or a Pieces alternative? If the missing feature is search, tagging or long-term snippet reuse, FloatBoard is not a direct replacement. If your problem is losing the screenshot while changing CSS, try a mixed reference board alongside your existing snippet library. Dash is another documentation and snippet tool, primarily for macOS, when API reference lookup is the main job.

sections.title: Use clipboard history for retrieval, the board for comparison
sections.html:
A clipboard manager can preserve recently copied material, including images in some products. A saved snippet adds information such as title, language and source. A floating board keeps selected material visible. These are different roles, and one app can support more than one role.

FloatBoard combines recent text clipboard history with a visible text-and-image board. The board lets you compare a screenshot with a pasted code fragment, but its clipboard history is not a versioned snippet library. Always compare an older clip with the current source before reusing it. See the clipboard workflow for the product details.

sections.title: Questions developers ask about snippets and screenshots
sections.html:
What is the best way to organize code snippets?

Keep production code in the repository. Save genuinely reusable fragments in a searchable snippet manager with a descriptive title, language, source link and date or version. Keep temporary debugging fragments in a small task board, then remove them when the issue is resolved.

Can a clipboard manager store images?

Some can; capabilities differ by product. FloatBoard lets you add images to its visible board and has recent text clipboard history. Do not assume its history stores every image you have copied. For a screenshot you must preserve, save the original in your project or issue tracker.

Is there a free alternative to Pieces for snippets?

massCode is a free, open-source snippet library, according to its official site. FloatBoard has a limited free plan for visible text-and-image references, but is not a Pieces replacement for searchable snippets or image-to-code extraction. Compare current plans and features on each official site.

What is the best code snippet manager for Windows?

There is no single best choice for every workflow. For a searchable local library, compare massCode with Cacher; for screenshot-to-code features, examine Pieces. For keeping a screenshot and the few relevant lines visible while you edit, FloatBoard can complement those tools. Try the task you actually repeat before committing your whole library.

sections.title: Keep the fix, clear the temporary board
sections.html:
When the issue is fixed, record the reproduction steps, changed file and before-and-after evidence in the issue or pull request. Store reusable snippets in the repository or a searchable library. Remove temporary references that no longer explain the task.

Try FloatBoard for a small UI debugging task with one screenshot, one snippet and one expected result. If the real pain is research notes rather than code, see the writing reference workflow.

title: How to Keep Research Notes Visible While Writing
description: Keep research notes beside Word or Google Docs without losing sources. Compare split screen, PowerToys and FloatBoard, then use a source-card template.
alt: FloatBoard showing text reference cards on the left and six image thumbnails on the right
caption: Text and image references can share a FloatBoard window. The screenshot shows the layout; the writing example below uses its own illustrative notes.
intro: To keep research notes visible while writing, separate the source from your own wording, then place only the two or three notes needed for the next paragraph beside your draft. On Windows you can use split screen, pin a notes window with PowerToys or use a purpose-built floating board. This guide shows when each works and how to avoid losing attribution while you write.

sections.title: Choose the notes needed for the next paragraph
sections.html:
Start with the claim you are about to write. Choose the source detail you must verify, a short quotation if exact wording matters and the question that paragraph should answer. Leave the rest of your research in its original library or project folder.

A useful working note answers four questions: where did this come from, when was it published or checked, what does it actually say, and how will I use it? A floating note is a prompt to check the original source, not a citation by itself.

For an image you plan to describe, record its source and what detail matters. The screenshot above shows FloatBoard text cards beside image thumbnails, but a text-only writing task does not need images.

sections.title: Three ways to keep notes beside Word or Google Docs
sections.html:
Use the least complicated setup that leaves your draft readable. These options solve the same visibility problem at different levels; the feature descriptions come from the linked product documentation, checked on 28 September 2026. This article is published by FloatBoard.

Choose a note setup for a writing session
SetupBest fitTrade-off
Split screenTwo windows are enough and you have room for both. Put the original source or notes beside your draft.On a narrow display, each window may become too small to read comfortably.
PowerToys Always On TopOn Windows, pin a notes window above the draft with the default Win+Ctrl+T shortcut.It pins an existing window; you still need to choose a notes app and keep source details organized yourself.
FloatBoardKeep short text notes and optional image reminders in one small window, then use its pin control while writing.It is a working board, not a citation manager or searchable research archive. The free plan includes 5 texts and 5 images per day.

Open the draft first. Place the reference so it does not cover the sentence you are editing. Switch back to the writing app and confirm the note stays visible. If it blocks the document, reduce the working set or use split screen instead.

sections.title: Copy this source-card structure before drafting
sections.html:
Imagine drafting a short product comparison. The following is a template, not a claim about any specific product:

Claim to check: [one factual statement]
Source: [author or organization + page title + URL]
Published/checked: [date shown by source / date you checked]
Exact wording: "[brief quotation, if needed]"
My paraphrase: [your own wording, clearly labelled]
Where it goes: [draft section or paragraph]
Before publishing: reopen source and verify context

Put the source and exact wording in one labelled note; keep your interpretation separately. If the page has changed, update the note from the original rather than trusting an old clipboard fragment. For product details about FloatBoard itself, verify against the feature overview, current plan and download page.

sections.title: Do not let a floating note become a lost citation
sections.html:
Use quotation marks for words copied exactly. Keep the original URL, author or organization and relevant publication date with the quote. When you paraphrase, compare your sentence with the full source passage; a short clipped phrase can reverse the meaning of a qualification.

For academic or citation-heavy writing, use a dedicated reference manager. Zotero integrates with word processors and can insert citations and bibliographies. FloatBoard does not replace that source library; it can hold a small visible working set while you consult Zotero or your documents.

If you are working with private correspondence or sensitive research, keep it out of screenshots that you share publicly. Only place material on the working board that is appropriate for that workspace.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions about visible writing notes
sections.html:
How can I keep notes always on top while writing in Windows?

Open your notes app and use Microsoft PowerToys Always On Top to pin its active window, or use FloatBoard’s own pin control. Resize the note window so Word or your browser stays readable.

Can I keep reference notes beside Google Docs?

Yes. Google Docs runs in a browser window, so you can place a separate notes window beside it or keep a small FloatBoard window pinned above it. If your screen is narrow, a side-by-side layout may work better than an overlapping note.

Should I use a floating note or Zotero for research?

Use Zotero or another reference manager for the source collection and final citations. Use a floating note for the few facts or questions you need in view during the current paragraph. A source card on the board should always point back to the original.

How do I avoid accidentally copying source text into my draft?

Label exact quotations and your own paraphrases differently. Draft from the source idea with the original closed or beside you, then reopen it to verify accuracy and attribution before publishing.

sections.title: Review the draft, then refresh the working set
sections.html:
At the end of the section, reopen each source and verify names, dates, numbers, qualifications and quotations. Move any lasting note into your source library or project document. Replace the temporary references with those needed for the next section.

Try FloatBoard with two source cards beside a draft, then decide whether a visible board improves your writing setup. If you mainly need to recover copied text, see the clipboard history guide; if you are comparing visual ideas, see the image reference workflow.

title: Windows Clipboard History: Copy Multiple Items and Keep Notes Visible
description: Learn how to use Win + V for copied text and images, troubleshoot missing clipboard items, and choose when floating notes help with an active task.
alt: FloatBoard window showing separate text cards beside a grid of image thumbnails
caption: FloatBoard displays text and image references together. This product screenshot illustrates the layout; it is not the Windows clipboard history panel.
intro: Press Windows + V to open clipboard history on Windows and reuse something you copied earlier. If you need instructions to stay in sight while completing a task, keep a short note in a separate visible window. This guide shows how to use both approaches, how to investigate missing clipboard entries, and how to avoid turning a temporary clipboard into your only record.

sections.title: How to copy and paste multiple items with Windows + V
sections.html:
1. Press Windows + V and turn on clipboard history if prompted.
  2. Copy a short piece of text, then copy a different one.
  3. Click where you want to insert the first item, reopen Windows + V, and select it.
  4. Repeat for another item. Check what was inserted before moving to the next field.

Microsoft documents a 25-entry history and a 4 MB limit per item, supporting text, HTML and bitmap formats. You can pin entries you want to retain. See Microsoft’s clipboard instructions, checked on 29 September 2026. These limits describe Windows clipboard history, not FloatBoard.

sections.title: Clipboard history or floating notes: which fits your task?
sections.html:
Choose by what you need to do next. Pasting a previously copied address is different from reading a checklist while you fill in a form. This comparison is published by FloatBoard and describes documented roles, not a performance benchmark.

Three ways to work with copied information
NeedUseful starting pointKeep in mind
Paste an earlier copyWindows clipboard historySelect an entry when you need to paste; check history limits.
Read a few notes while workingFloatBoard’s floating text and image windowKeep only the references for the current task; check plan limits.
Keep a lasting project recordYour project document or notes librarySave sources, final wording and decisions where you can find them later.

You can use clipboard history and a visible note together. There is no need to move your entire history into a board.

sections.title: Example: prepare a product listing without mixing up fields
sections.html:
Imagine updating a listing with an approved name, a short description and an image. The goal is to check each field against its source while editing. The following is an illustrative workflow, not a report of a measured time saving.

  1. Open the approved source document and the listing editor.
  2. Create a small FloatBoard text note with labels for the title, description and items to verify.
  3. Add the relevant image reference if you need to check the selected picture. Keep the original file for the actual upload.
  4. Use the board’s pin control and position the window beside the editor. Switch back to the editor to confirm the note stays visible.
  5. Paste each field, using Windows clipboard history when helpful, then compare the result against the labelled note.
  6. Read the final preview and save the approved version in the project document.
LISTING CHECK
Title: [approved wording]
Description source: [document / section]
Image: [original filename]
Before saving: spelling, selected image, required fields

Labels matter: two similar copied sentences can belong to different products. Keep one listing’s working set on screen at a time.

sections.title: Why is an item missing from Windows clipboard history?
sections.html:
First check whether history was enabled when you copied it. Then check the item’s format and size. An older entry may have been displaced by the history limit. Microsoft also notes that restarting clears unpinned history. Its clipboard support page explains pinning and clearing entries.

If a particular image does not appear, keep its original file and insert it through the destination app’s image command. Do not keep recopying a large file and assume the history panel will store it. If the entry appears but the pasted result looks wrong, inspect the destination’s paste options and compare against the source.

A visible reference is useful for checking the result, but it cannot repair an unsupported clipboard format or reconstruct information that was never saved.

sections.title: Keep the working set small and labelled
sections.html:
Before a new task, remove references that belong to the previous one. Preserve anything important in your project files first. Avoid copying passwords or other secrets into a board that might appear in a screen share.

FloatBoard’s free plan currently allows five texts and five images per day and one window. A note containing a few labelled fields is enough to try this workflow. This article does not claim that FloatBoard provides Windows clipboard synchronization or an unlimited free history.

sections.title: Questions about clipboard history and floating notes
sections.html:
Does Windows + V show everything I have ever copied?

No. It is a limited history, not a permanent archive. Keep important material in a saved document and use the history for recent copied items.

Can clipboard history contain images?

Windows clipboard history supports bitmap content within its size limit. That does not mean every copied image or file format will be stored. Keep the original image when you need dependable access.

Can I keep copied text visible without repeatedly opening the history?

Put the relevant text in a note window. FloatBoard can keep a small text-and-image working set above other windows. If you already have the note in another app, a window-pinning tool may be enough.

What should I try first?

Try Windows + V for reuse. If the real problem is losing sight of instructions, try FloatBoard with one labelled note and read the clipboard workspace guide. For code and screenshots, follow the separate UI debugging workflow.

title: How to Take Notes While Watching a Tutorial on One Screen
description: Use a timestamp, next-action note and screenshot to follow a software tutorial on one monitor. Compare split screen, PowerToys and floating notes.
alt: FloatBoard displaying image thumbnails next to a text panel containing an HTML reference snippet
caption: A FloatBoard text-and-image layout can hold references for a learning task. This existing product screenshot shows the interface, not a capture of the tutorial example below.
intro: When following a software tutorial on one screen, keep three things in your notes: the timestamp, the next action to try, and the result you expect. Pause to practise each step, then record what actually happened. A split-screen layout or a small floating note can keep those instructions visible beside your app without copying the entire lesson.

sections.title: Choose one result to reproduce
sections.html:
Before playing the tutorial, write down what you want to make: a responsive card, an image export or a spreadsheet formula. Record the tutorial URL and the software version used by the instructor if it is shown. Menu names and features can differ between versions.

For this example, suppose you are learning to build a card that changes from two columns to one on a narrow screen. You need the relevant breakpoint and layout rule, not a transcript of the whole video. Keep the completed exercise in your project folder.

sections.title: Split screen, PowerToys or FloatBoard?
sections.html:
Start with the layout that leaves your working app readable. The options below serve different needs; this is a FloatBoard product guide, not an independent comparative test.

Ways to keep tutorial instructions in sight
LayoutBest fitTrade-off
Side-by-side windowsWatching the instructor while practisingBoth apps need enough width to show their controls.
PowerToys Always On TopKeeping an existing note app visible on WindowsIt pins a window; your chosen app still handles the notes.
FloatBoardKeeping a short action note beside a screenshot or copied referenceA compact working set fits better than an entire lesson transcript.

With PowerToys installed and Always On Top enabled, select a note window and press Windows + Ctrl + T, the default shortcut, to toggle pinning. See Microsoft’s instructions, checked on 29 September 2026. If you changed the shortcut, use your configured combination.

sections.title: A tutorial note template you can copy
sections.html:
LESSON: [title + URL]
SOFTWARE: [app and version]
TIMESTAMP: [mm:ss]
GOAL: [one result]
NEXT ACTION: [one thing to try]
EXPECTED: [what should change]
ACTUAL: [what happened]
QUESTION: [what remains unclear]

For the responsive-card example, the next action could be: ‘Change the grid to one column below the chosen breakpoint.’ The expected result is: ‘Image appears above the text without horizontal scrolling.’ If it does not work, record the viewport width and the observed result before changing another rule.

The timestamp points back to the explanation. The actual-result line preserves your own observation. Keeping those separate helps you distinguish what the instructor said from what your project did.

sections.title: Follow a watch, pause, practise and check cycle
sections.html:
1. Watch one meaningful step. Stop when the instructor completes an action you can reproduce.
  2. Write the action in your own words. Copy a command only when exact spelling matters, and keep its source.
  3. Put the note in view. In FloatBoard, add your short text note, use the pin control and place the window beside your working area.
  4. Practise with the video paused. Return to your app and complete that single action.
  5. Compare the result. If a visual detail matters, keep one relevant screenshot alongside the note. Check small details in the original image.
  6. Record the outcome. Write what worked or the question to revisit, then advance to the next step.

Try this with one note and one image first. FloatBoard’s free plan has daily text and image limits, so use the board for the active step and your saved notes for the full lesson. The window does not need to contain every screenshot you take.

sections.title: What to do when the tutorial and your result differ
sections.html:
A menu item is missing: compare your software version with the lesson before trying unrelated commands. Note the version difference and consult that app’s documentation.

Your output looks different: compare at the same viewport size, zoom level or export setting. A screenshot without those conditions can lead you to fix the wrong thing.

The note covers a control: move or resize the note, or temporarily unpin it. If you constantly need to uncover the app, switch to side-by-side windows or pause the video more often.

You have too many unanswered questions: save them in the lesson document. Keep only the question blocking the current step in the floating note. For a reproducible interface problem, the code-and-screenshot debugging guide offers a more detailed evidence template.

sections.title: Turn the temporary note into a useful record
sections.html:
At the end of a lesson, save three things together: your exercise, the source URL with useful timestamps, and a short explanation of the step you can now perform. Move unresolved questions into that record before clearing the board.

Use screenshots you are allowed to retain and do not redistribute a paid course’s materials without permission. A screenshot can remind you where a control was, but your own explanation is what makes the note reusable when the interface changes.

sections.title: Questions about taking notes during tutorials
sections.html:
Should I write down everything the instructor says?

For a practical software task, begin with the action, expected result and question you need answered. Add background explanation when it changes how you perform the task. A full transcript can be useful for other purposes, but it is hard to use as a small on-screen checklist.

How can I take notes without a second monitor?

Pause the lesson while practising, use side-by-side windows when space allows, or keep a short note pinned above your app. Change the layout if it makes controls too small to use comfortably.

Does FloatBoard automatically transcribe or synchronize a video?

This workflow uses manually written notes, timestamps and selected image references. It does not depend on transcription, a video integration or automatic timestamp capture.

Can I use this for reading a written tutorial?

Yes. Replace the timestamp with the heading or section link. For longer reading and drafting, use the research notes workflow. To try the compact tutorial setup, download FloatBoard and start with a single next-action note.
